reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / IDSA
clinicalPearls: Most often affects the superficial olecranon and prepatellar bursae, which are prone to trauma and abrasion
Infection usually follows direct inoculation through breached skin rather than haematogenous spread
Staphylococcus aureus is the predominant organism, with beta-haemolytic streptococci next most common
Distinguishing septic from non-septic (crystal, traumatic, or inflammatory) bursitis is the central clinical challenge and may require bursal fluid aspiration
Overlying warmth, erythema, tenderness, and fever favour infection but can be mimicked by gout or trauma
Unlike septic arthritis, passive joint movement is typically well preserved because the bursa lies outside the joint
Management principles combine aspiration for diagnosis, antistaphylococcal antibiotics, and drainage of persistent or loculated collections
Recurrent or refractory cases may need surgical bursectomy, and predisposing occupational trauma should be addressed
reference.pathophysiology: A bursa is a synovial-lined sac that reduces friction over bony prominences. Superficial bursae such as the olecranon and prepatellar sit just beneath the skin and are readily seeded by direct trauma or overlying cellulitis. Introduced bacteria, usually skin flora, provoke an inflammatory exudate within the bursal cavity, producing pain, swelling, warmth, and sometimes abscess formation. Because the bursa is anatomically separate from the joint, infection tends to remain localised unless it extends into surrounding tissue.
additionalDifferentials: Septic arthritis of the adjacent joint
infectionMimics: Acute gouty bursitis or tophaceous deposits
additionalInvestigations: Aspiration of bursal fluid for Gram stain, culture, cell count, and crystal analysis
Blood cultures and inflammatory markers when systemic signs are present
Comparison of bursal fluid findings with adjacent joint fluid if joint infection is a concern
Ultrasound to confirm a bursal collection and guide aspiration
Assessment for underlying immunosuppression or predisposing trauma
redFlags: Spread into the adjacent joint or deep tissues suggesting septic arthritis or deeper infection
Systemic sepsis or rapidly advancing surrounding cellulitis requiring urgent treatment
Failure to improve after aspiration and antibiotics indicating a loculated or abscessed collection needing drainage
Immunocompromised host in whom infection may progress atypically or rapidly
reference.prognosis: Superficial septic bursitis generally resolves well with aspiration and appropriate antibiotics; recurrence or chronicity is more likely with repeated trauma or delayed treatment, and a minority require surgical bursectomy.
pitfalls: Assuming an inflamed bursa is gouty or traumatic and missing infection
Confusing septic bursitis with septic arthritis, which requires more aggressive intervention
Injecting corticosteroid into a bursa without excluding infection
Stopping treatment prematurely and precipitating relapse
management: Aspirate the infected bursa for both diagnostic fluid analysis and therapeutic decompression
Start empirical antistaphylococcal antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus and beta-haemolytic streptococci, narrowing therapy to culture and sensitivity results
Repeat aspiration for reaccumulation and reserve surgical bursectomy or incision and drainage for abscess formation or refractory infection
Provide supportive analgesia, rest, and elevation of the affected limb
Address predisposing factors such as recurrent trauma over the bursa and underlying immunosuppression
Escalate for admission and intravenous therapy if there is spreading cellulitis, systemic sepsis, or failure to respond to oral treatment
